rv.q: If you can afford it, Sarah Jessica Parker – with Broderick as Ken to her Barbie – is worth it.
The public appetite for this show...stems greatly from Parker's presence.
Their performances feel intimate as well as expansive.
But it’s not quite enough to blow the dust off the play and its creakily dated depiction of the sexes.
The jokes feel effortful and small “c” conservative: landing them would be a stretch for far more accomplished stage actors than Parker and Broderick, who are just about good enough here.
It’s a theatrical museum piece, barely in working order, dusty and decidedly creaky.
The production is flat and forgettable, not testing either actor’s seasoned skills on the boards.
I could not wait to check out of Plaza Suite.
Matthew Broderick and Sarah Jessica Parker...are doing coathanger acting, encased in a set by John Lee Beatty that is both doggedly realistic and flimsy.
This is exactly the lavish comedy we need to lift our spirits, led by a starry dream team: a full-service romp.
You laugh heartily at the accelerating insanity of the piece even as you clock the darkness attendant behind it.
Sarah Jessica Parker is a revelation - she is pitch-perfect in each act, expertly judging the tone required and effortlessly balancing the humour and the drama involved.
Even Parker can’t get this stale, clichéd story off the ground.
Overall, this revival is a mixed bag with a glittering exterior.
The dialogue sounds true to life but it’s also meandering, flat and witless – the sort of drivel you’d overhear in a vet’s waiting room.
Sarah Jessica Parker brings sublimity to the city in this powerhouse performance.
Even though I chuckled throughout, the more I thought about it all afterwards, the less funny I found it.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this star-powered revival: some find Parker and Broderick's chemistry delightful in Simon's triptych, while others deem the 1968 comedy dated and the eye-watering ticket prices hard to justify.
